description: THIS IS A TEAM FROM MTC COLLEGE OF OMAN, PRIVATE TEAM MEMEBERS
summary:
ATHAR (أثر, “trace”) is a bilingual (English/Arabic) web platform that turns NASA Earth-observation data into trustworthy trend findings. For any location, it ranks 11 NASA POWER variables (MERRA-2 reanalysis and CERES satellite radiation, 1981–2025) by how strongly they are changing. It then tests each trend with a Mann–Kendall test corrected for year-to-year memory, a Theil–Sen slope with a confidence interval, a Pettitt change-point check that flags artificial data steps, and false-discovery control across all variables. A case file in English and Arabic is generated from the test results, so no number is invented. A map view, a “compare places” view, and a user-data upload let teams test their own series.

It answers the challenge by showing which variables are changing, where, by how much, and whether each trend is real or just noise. An “Honesty Lab” simulates trendless data to measure false-alarm rates (about 6% with our correction, against 16–24% for uncorrected tests).

It matters because Earth data is huge and noisy, and weak or accidental trends can mislead decisions. ATHAR helps students, planners, and scientists look in the right place, and it does so in Arabic, a language that science tools rarely serve.
details:
What it does and how it works

ATHAR (أثر, “trace”) is a free, bilingual web platform that answers four questions about any Earth-system time series: what is changing, where, by how much, and is the trend real. It uses annual means from 1981 to 2025 for 11 NASA POWER variables (MERRA-2 and CERES) at 10 places, six of them in Oman. It works in four steps:

  1. Triage ranks all variables for a place by a detectability score.
  2. Test runs a Mann–Kendall test corrected for year-to-year memory, a Theil–Sen slope with a 95% confidence interval, a change-point check, and false-discovery control across variables.
  3. Case file writes the result in plain Arabic and English: what, where, how much, is it real, and a caveat.
  4. Honesty lab simulates trendless data to measure ATHAR’s own false-alarm rate.

For example, wind speed at Ibra rises by +0.052 m/s per decade (p < 0.0001). ATHAR also flags that most of the change sits around 2013, a possible data-source step, instead of over-claiming.

Benefits

  • It prevents false discoveries. Climate series have memory, so in our simulation a plain trend test reported a trend on trendless data 23.6% of the time. ATHAR’s corrected test reports one 6.5% of the time, close to the 5% target.
  • It is fully usable in Arabic, which science tools rarely support.
  • It runs in the browser with no server, even offline, and users can upload their own CSV series.

Intended impact

Students, teachers and local planners can explore NASA data and judge for themselves whether a trend is real, without a statistics background. It also teaches that a significant trend can still come from a change in the data source.

Tools and technologies

  • Python for the statistical engine, a Streamlit app, and 10 automated tests.
  • Vanilla JavaScript, HTML, CSS and SVG charts for the website. The JavaScript engine was ported from Python and checked to give the same results.
  • NASA POWER API as the data source, and GitHub and GitHub Pages for hosting and open-source code.
  • AI-assisted development: we used Claude as a coding and writing assistant. All results come from the statistical tests, not from a language model.

No special hardware was needed.

Creativity

Most tools show a trend. ATHAR shows how much to trust it. It measures its own error rate live in the browser, flags suspected data steps, and writes the evidence as a readable case file in two languages.

Factors we considered

  • Statistical honesty: autocorrelation, multiple testing across 11 variables, and change points that may be instrument artifacts.
  • Accessibility: right-to-left Arabic, a phone layout, and offline use.
  • Transparency and reproducibility: open code, tests, and bundled data.
  • Limits: annual means and a modest sample size, which the platform states openly.
dataRefs: NASA POWER (Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources)
